t019: Halo is an open-source AI assistant for Android today, built around a portable runtime for future hosts. Ask by voice or text, try supported phone actions, save notes, files and voice memos in Notebook, arrange them on Canvas, and learn from selected sources in Study. Choose a compatible on-device model, your own network server or an optional cloud provider. Glasses are optional. This alpha still has unverified workflows.

t126: Notebook keeps notes, files, conversations and collections together. Canvas supports source-linked cards, voice memos, drawings, image tools and selected PDF-page extraction in code. Check transcripts and OCR results against the originals; some workflows still require device testing.
t128: Study can build a session from selected material, give guided explanations and practice, save attempts and review progress. Availability of narration, image understanding and model feedback depends on your configured capabilities.
t131: Notebook storage and cognitive memory are separate concepts. Promoting something into memory is a distinct action, not an automatic side effect of writing a note.
t133: Start on Android. Other devices are optional.
t134: Android works as a standalone host. Devices shows the phone first, then optional glasses, headsets and experimental hardware. A listed capability is not proof that a device is connected or permitted to act.
t138: The Android app includes Home, Activity, Notebook, model and voice setup, supported phone tools, and Study. New layouts and device-sensitive workflows still need hands-on validation.
t141: HeyCyan glasses are an active Bluetooth and microphone integration target. Pairing and basic device status have dedicated screens; speaker routing and media paths still need hands-on verification.
t144: Supported Android headsets can provide microphone and audio output, depending on routing and permissions.
t146: BuddyBot is a robot project exploring physical actions and safety. It is experimental and not needed to use Halo.
t148: One runtime, different devices and models.
t149: Halo separates input, context, model reasoning, permissions and tool execution. Android is the first host; Linux and Windows are development targets, not released apps. The aim is to keep the assistant useful without committing to a single model or gadget.
t162: Connected devices report what they can do. Halo does not assume every device has the same sensors or controls.

heroOrbCaption: Halo at rest · the open ring
missionTitle: An assistant that fits into your day.
missionBody: Halo brings together everyday requests, supported phone actions, notes and learning on Android. You decide which sources and permissions it can use, and whether a request goes to an on-device model or a service you select.
missionPill1Body: A compatible model can answer on your phone after you download and test it. Available memory, performance and supported languages depend on the device and model.
missionPill2Body: The opening in the ring stands for an open project. The Android app, runtime and website can be examined and improved by contributors.
missionPill3Body: Your files stay local unless you choose an action or provider that shares information. Review permissions and the privacy terms of any service you connect.
ringIntro: The open gap is deliberate: Halo is designed to remain approachable and open to contribution.
ringGapBody: Halo is built in the open, with room for anyone to contribute.
ringRingTitle: The ring is a halo of light.
ringRingBody: A quiet visual signal for assistance, not another screen that demands attention.
ringGradientTitle: The gradient suggests near to far.
ringGradientBody: It represents the journey from the device towards optional cloud computing. It is symbolic, not a live indicator of where a specific request was sent.
ringEndsBody: Simple shapes keep the mark friendly without turning it into a cartoon character.
ringCaption: The gap and centre symbol change with the state.
presenceMotionNote: Fifteen of the 21 states are animated in the brand kit. The other six are shown as stills.
layersIntro: Presence never changes because of where the answer comes from. Context and conditions ride along as badges, so the ring always means the same thing.
layer1Body: The ring and its glyph. Set by what Halo is doing, never by which model is answering.
layer2Body: Where the turn is running, or what it is using. One badge, bottom right.
layer3Body: Something you need to know or act on. One badge, bottom left, and it wins attention over context.
stateIdleInfo: The ring stays still with its opening at the upper right. Halo is ready for a new request.
stateListeningInfo: The ring brightens and a dot pulses, only while the microphone is open.
stateCapturingVoiceInfo: Five bars move with your voice while Halo records what you said.
stateCapturingVisionInfo: The aperture turns while the camera is capturing, and not before.
stateThinkingInfo: The opening moves around the ring while a model works on the reply.
statePlanningInfo: A short plan is drawn up before a multi-step task starts.
stateActingInfo: Three segments advance, one for each stage of the running task.
stateActingPhoneInfo: A phone glyph shows that the step happens on the device itself.
stateSpeakingInfo: Ripples travel outward, but only while audio is actually playing.
stateStreamingTextInfo: Three lines draw on in sequence for a reply with no audio.
statePreparingContextInfo: Halo gathers the material the current question needs.
stateWaitingInfo: The ring dims and an apricot dot breathes while Halo waits.
stateApprovalRequiredInfo: An apricot arc marks a step that will not run without you.
stateSuccessInfo: The gap closes into a full ring, a check draws on, and the state holds.
stateWarningInfo: An apricot arc appears next to the glyph and stays until you look.
stateErrorInfo: Ember is the only error colour, and it always arrives with a glyph.
stateRecoveringInfo: A retry arrow can repeat one step instead of work that already finished.
stateModelLoadingInfo: A progress arc follows the real download percentage.
statePermissionMissingInfo: The ring dims and holds a lock until a permission is granted.
stateOfflineInfo: A dashed ring means no connection is available right now.
stateStoppedInfo: A stopped ring holds a square until you start something new.
productFlowTitle: Start simple. Add more when you're ready.
productSetupBody: Choose a language, decide where replies come from, and test the permissions and voice options you want. You can save progress and finish setup later.
productKidsBody: A simpler Home layout connects questions and guided learning to the same Study system. Parent controls and device testing still need review; do not treat it as an unsupervised safety boundary.
productModelsBody: Find and test compatible local LiteRT models. Speech recognition and voice output have their own model setup; no download automatically makes a model your default.
brandUpdateTitle: Devices, permissions and settings — explained clearly.
brandUpdateIntro: The updated design book covers device discovery, pairing and the Intelligence, Voice and Privacy settings. The examples below show intended layouts, not verified captures from a released APK.
brandUpdateTag: DESIGN REFERENCE · NOT A LIVE BUILD
brandUpdateFoot: Artwork from the supplied Brand Book, pages 42–45; screenshots elsewhere on this page are from an earlier Android test build. These two sources are intentionally labeled differently.
phoneAbilitiesBody: Devices now groups the phone's reported capabilities into categories. “Available” means the runtime reported a capability; it is not a grant to read private information or control the phone. Permissions and confirmations remain separate.
pairingBody: Allow nearby-device access if Android asks, search for powered-on glasses, select the right result, then connect. A successful connection does not automatically start recording, camera capture or audio routing.
